paras: The West Sixty-second Street riot was a clash on the evening of Sunday, July 12, 1903, between New York policemen and Black residents of the tenement block on West Sixty-second Street between West End and Amsterdam avenues, set off by a patrolman's attempt to arrest a Black man. Bricks and shots were exchanged, reserves from three police stations cleared the street, and two Black men, William Johnson and William Brackett, were among those arrested; no deaths were reported. Wire services carried it nationally as a "race riot," and a report that white crowds had attacked Black people in the neighborhood drew Southern editorial comment.

According to Policeman Connor, whose account the New-York Tribune printed, Black men standing beside a saloon at No. 236 threatened him at about six o'clock, and when he ordered them to move, William Johnson struck him on the neck. Connor clubbed and seized Johnson, and as he led him away men on the roof of No. 239 threw bricks, one striking Connor on the leg. After two more policemen arrived, Connor fired at a man on the roof; two men fired back from a window, and the Tribune said a white passer-by returned their fire.

Connor arrested William Brackett on the roof, accusing him of throwing bricks, then reached a patrol box, "cracking the head of every man who stood in his way." Captain Kear and reserves from three stations cleared the street and chased people over the roofs; the Associated Press reported "several arrests."

Reserves were called to the block again on Monday night, July 13, after Patrick H. Harrington said two Black men had held him up and hit him with a brick and Policeman Kelly arrested Charles Naething, 17. The Sun reported that some thirty policemen found no riot, and Captain Kear said there was no better way to start trouble "than to fire a lot of policemen into it." Alarmed by the police, a delegation of Black residents asked a local Republican club for protection, which the station sergeant promised.

A wire dispatch dated July 14 instead described a "resumption of the race rioting" in which young Black men beat Harrington and, once the police left, white crowds attacked every Black person in sight and severely beat several. No report of court proceedings against those arrested, or of arrests of white attackers, was found.

The Tribune ran the story on its front page as "NEGROES BESET POLICE," told from Connor's side and ending with the policemen's wish for their long night sticks. The Associated Press version, calling Johnson "the leader of a gang of negroes," ran on July 13 in the Saint Paul Globe as "POLICE BATTLE WITH BLACKS OVER ROOFS" and in the Indianapolis Journal and New Haven Morning Journal and Courier. It also appeared in the Alexandria Gazette, the Daily New Dominion, the Butte Inter Mountain and, as one line, the San Antonio Daily Light.

The Sun headlined its July 14 report "MANY COPS, NO RACE RIOT" and blamed a patrolman who had "lost his head." Headlines on the July 14 wire differed in emphasis: "Negroes Who Beat a White Man Are Driven From the Streets" in the Minneapolis Journal, "White Mob Attacks Every Black Person in Sight" in the Topeka State Journal. Southern papers used the reports against Northern critics of lynching; the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic said New York race riots had "become an almost daily occurrence," and the White Oaks Eagle quoted a remark that "the recent race riot in New York" was "clearly the result of race prejudice."

No Black-press report of this riot was found; the Colored American's New York letter of July 18, headed "Race Riots in New York," described a separate clash on 133d Street in which seven Black men and no white men were arrested. Its correspondent protested that it was "an unheard-of occurrence for a white man to be clubbed for attacking a Negro."

The account of the Sunday riot comes from police sources, chiefly Connor, and no version from the arrested men or other residents appears. For Monday night, The Sun, a local paper naming those involved, found "no riot," while the wire reported white crowds beating Black residents without naming a source.

reader.title: West Sixty-second Street riot (New York, 1903)
bases: The core event is a patrolman's arrest of a Black man that became a fight between police (clubs, revolver fire, reserves of three stations) and Black residents throwing bricks (A1, A2); a wire report of white crowds attacking Black people two days later (A10, A15) is disputed by the local Sun (A9).

The Tribune's own report (A1) and the Associated Press dispatch (A2, A6, A7) agree on the place, Connor, Johnson's arrest, bricks from the roofs, gunfire and the reserves, and the Sun refers to the Sunday 'muss' (A9); all of these rest on police accounts.

accounts.label: Policeman Connor via the New-York Tribune
accounts.gist: A disorderly crowd threatened Connor; Johnson struck him; residents rained bricks and fired from a window; Connor shot back and clubbed his way to a call box.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Connor's attempt to arrest Johnson, 'leader of a gang', set off a riot needing reserves of three precincts; shots were exchanged and several arrests made.

accounts.label: The Sun on the second night
accounts.gist: An excited patrolman called reserves after an arrest drew a crowd; thirty police found no riot, and Black residents sought protection from a Republican club.

accounts.label: July 14 wire on renewed rioting
accounts.gist: Young Black men beat Alderman Harrington's son; after police left, white crowds attacked every Black person in sight and beat several.

accounts.label: Colored American correspondent
accounts.gist: In New York race riots Black people are always the ones clubbed and arrested; describes a separate 133d Street clash in which seven Black men and no white men were arrested.

framing.detail: The Tribune's 'NEGROES BESET POLICE / USE PISTOLS AND BRICKS' tells the story from Connor's side, closes on the policemen's wish for their long night sticks.
AP headlines such as 'POLICE BATTLE WITH BLACKS OVER ROOFS' and 'POLICE FIGHT NEGRO RIOTERS' call Johnson a gang leader.
The Sun's 'MANY COPS, NO RACE RIOT' blames an excitable patrolman and reports Black residents' request for protection.

The July 14 wire ran under headlines that led either with the Black men's attack ('Negroes Who Beat a White Man Are Driven From the Streets') or the white crowd ('White Mob Attacks Every Black Person in Sight').
Southern editorials (Pine Bluff, White Oaks) used New York's riots to charge Northern hypocrisy about Southern lynching.
The Colored American's New York letter, headed 'Race Riots in New York', protested that only Black people were clubbed and arrested.
